stories.topic: Mark Carney: From the Bank of England to Prime Minister of Canada, via Donald Trump
stories.summary: In 2012, after scandals in the UK, Britain's appointment process chose a Canadian, Mark Carney, to run its central bank. This worked because both countries have mature statistics, sound models and strong research teams, so inflation targeting in Canada is much like inflation targeting in the UK. Carney later went home and entered party politics. Then two 'miracles' happened. Trudeau's popularity collapsed, which opened space for a right-wing nationalist. Then Trump threatened to annex Canada as the next US state, and angry Canadians voted for any plausible candidate who was not a right-wing conservative. That candidate turned out to be Carney.
stories.insight: Manmohan Singh was appointed at every step. Carney won fair and square through the constitution, and that gives him a different level of authority. But a technocrat with little knowledge of party machines may have been lifted by a one-off moment. Whether he can win again once Trump matters less is an open question.
stories.quote: Okay, so Donald Trump is the critical divine intervention that got Mark Carney to power.

stories.topic: Nehru's Congress: When Chief Ministers Could Say No
stories.summary: In the late 1940s, a Ram idol was placed inside the Babri Masjid. An aghast Nehru asked UP chief minister Govind Ballabh Pant to remove it ('isko hatao'). Pant refused, and so did UP's home minister at the time, Lal Bahadur Shastri. In Nehru's era, state legislators elected their own chief minister and party politics ran bottom-up. Amit argues that Indira Gandhi later hollowed out the Congress by removing and appointing chief ministers at will.
stories.insight: A prime minister being refused by his own party's state leaders was a sign of institutional health. A party that becomes an extension of one leader's will turns into a toothless shell.
stories.quote: That is unimaginable in the modern time, where you know, if the same party is in rule at the center in the state, the people at the state are basically vassals.

stories.topic: Havel's Notebook: 'Questions I Cannot Answer'
stories.summary: The communists branded Havel's well-to-do family class enemies, so he was barred from studying philosophy at university. He took a job as a lab technician there just to be near it. Michael Zantovsky's biography describes him arriving in overalls, pockets stuffed with Kafka, Camus, Heidegger and Nietzsche, and writing alone in a battered journal during breaks while co-workers joked that he was a professor. Amit also recalls, from memory and without being able to find it online, a friend's story: Havel was scribbling furiously in a notebook, and as he closed it the friend saw its title, 'Questions I Cannot Answer'.
stories.insight: Blocked from the formal path, Havel educated himself anyway. The notebook title captures what Amit admires most: deep curiosity paired with deep humility.
stories.quote: Right, so immediately you have a sense of both deep curiosity and deep humility from someone who is obviously an incredibly smart man.

stories.topic: Charter 77: 'You Have Already Taken a Side'
stories.summary: In 1977 Havel co-authored Charter 77 and wanted many Czechoslovaks to sign it. One fellow traveller said she agreed with it but felt signing was dangerous and wasn't sure she should take a side. Havel told her she had already taken one, just not the one she thought. She signed. Decades later, campaigning in 2008 for the Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo to get the Nobel Prize, Havel said the crimes of the twentieth century began when good men stayed silent.
stories.insight: Neutrality under oppression is an illusion. Staying silent is itself a choice that favours the oppressor, so a citizen's duty goes beyond not doing evil to actually speaking up.
stories.quote: And Havel famously told her, that you have already taken a side, just not the one that you think you have. And then she signed.

stories.topic: Havel, the President Who Refused to Become a Politician
stories.summary: Havel spent four continuous years in prison (1979–83). After the Velvet Revolution he formed the Civic Forum, a motley crew of civil-society figures; one fellow dissident said they had 'no plan, no money, no weapons. Only Havel's calm voice and his moral authority.' As president he would not move into the presidential palace and stayed in his humble flat. Amit contrasts this with Arvind Kejriwal, who made noises about refusing an official bungalow and then had a palatial house refurbished. Havel also refused to wear a tie. When a reporter asked why the president had dishevelled hair and a messy jacket, Havel said he represented the people, and the people were like that. And instead of filling his calendar with summits, he invited Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones to perform.
stories.insight: Authenticity in office means refusing to let the role turn you into its uniform. Amit draws the Indian parallel of the white kurta-pyjama, worn by many only because it is what politicians wear.
stories.quote: Because I represent the people. The people are like this. Why should I be different from them?

stories.topic: Havel vs Lee Kuan Yew: 'Then I Shall Tell Him He Is Wrong'
stories.summary: Salil Tripathi, telling the story on The Seen and the Unseen, was at a press conference with Havel, who was due to meet Lee Kuan Yew that afternoon. Salil asked Havel about the view that free speech matters less than feeding a hungry person. Havel said he disagreed: without free speech, how would a hungry person say they are hungry? Then he asked who held that view. Salil replied that it was the person he was meeting that afternoon. The room went silent. Havel said he would make sure to tell Lee he was wrong.
stories.insight: Meetings between heads of state are usually choreographed and diplomatic. Havel's way of doing things was to stay true to himself, even when holding power.
stories.quote: If you do not have free speech, how will a hungry person be able to say that they are hungry?

stories.topic: Katyn: Why Tyrants Hunt Thinkers
stories.summary: When the Soviet army invaded Poland in 1939 and met the German army, splitting the country roughly in half, the Soviets came with a list of Polish intellectuals, leaders, thinkers and scientists. These people were seized, taken to a camp called Katyn in the USSR, and killed one by one.
stories.insight: Occupiers understand that a country's thinking elite is the source of its long-term strength. Destroy that class and the country stays weak, which makes it easier to dominate. That is why people like Havel matter so disproportionately.
stories.quote: If you can destroy the thinking elite of a country, then you've really done tremendous long term damage to that country.

stories.topic: Nehru's 'Chanakya' Letter Against Himself
stories.summary: While Nehru was prime minister, a letter signed 'Chanakya' appeared in the Hindustan Times. It warned that Nehru was becoming a Julius Caesar: power had concentrated in him, he was surrounded by sycophants, he dismissed people with a wave of his hand, and readers should get together and dethrone him. Years later it emerged that Nehru himself had written it.
stories.insight: Ajay calls it his favourite Nehru story. A sitting leader publicly sounding the alarm about his own power is the opposite of a politician's instinct, and it shows a man genuinely worried about concentrated power.
stories.quote: Can you imagine a sitting prime minister of India publishing an article saying that this Prime Minister has become too powerful and this is not a healthy state of affairs.

stories.topic: Nehru the Writer: Jail Notebooks and a Speech on Tissue Paper
stories.summary: Nehru spent nine years in British jails. There was no heating or air conditioning, but he had books and notebooks and was not beaten, a decency the British did not extend to Savarkar. He used the time to read and write, producing Glimpses of World History as letters to his daughter, and The Discovery of India. Tryst with Destiny, which Salman Rushdie made chapter one of his anthology of Indian writing, was scribbled on a random piece of tissue paper about fifteen minutes before the speech.
stories.insight: Tryst with Destiny has become a cliché, but read with fresh eyes it shows a thinker, dreamer and idealist rather than a normal politician. Nehru turned prison into a workshop for ideas.
stories.quote: Here you have a man literally fifteen minutes before the speech, scribbling on some random piece of tissue paper, and look at the writing.

stories.topic: The Chain of Accidents That Made Nehru Prime Minister
stories.summary: Nehru was a highly educated, English-speaking returnee from the UK with no obvious political career ahead of him. Without the First World War, the Great Depression, the Second World War and the Atlantic Charter, Ajay argues, the British would not have left in 1947, and if they had stayed twenty more years it would not have been Nehru's time. Gandhi then picked him out of a galaxy of great people as the dreamer and philosopher he wanted. Amit adds that Gandhi's main reason for choosing him over the free-market-loving Rajaji was that Nehru was much younger, yet Rajaji outlived him. Nehru then won genuine mass popularity: people trekked for a week to catch a glimpse of him, with no big screens and barely any loudspeakers.
stories.insight: Even a towering 'natural' leader was an accident of history. Decent people choosing decent people, rather than realpolitik, put him there.
stories.quote: It takes a Gandhi to choose a Nehru.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh's PhD: Indians Can Export
stories.summary: In the 1960s, Indian economists broadly agreed that India, being India, was incapable of exporting. In his PhD thesis, Manmohan Singh was one of the first to challenge this. He argued that export success depends on incentives such as prices, customs duties and exchange rates, so with the right policies there was no reason India could not export.
stories.insight: The quiet technocrat began as an iconoclast. Fatalistic beliefs about a nation's 'nature' often turn out to be the result of bad policy.
stories.quote: Success in exporting is shaped by incentives. It's about prices, it's about customs duties, it's about exchange rates.

stories.topic: Percy Mistry's Million-Pound Cheque
stories.summary: Manmohan Singh was to head the South-South Commission in Geneva when Ronald Reagan cut off UN funding, leaving him with no money to function or build the institution. Percy Mistry wrote a personal cheque for a million pounds as a loan to the commission, which got it started. When funding later resumed, the money was repaid.
stories.insight: Ajay offers it as an example of a bigger-scale generation, people who personally underwrote public-spirited projects when institutions failed.
stories.quote: Those were men at a bigger scale.

stories.topic: 1991: When Nobody Gave a Damn About India
stories.summary: By the late-1980s balance of payments crisis, policy confusion between the RBI and the Finance Ministry had run India into a wall. Imports had stalled, life-saving drugs and raw materials couldn't come in, and factories were closing. Reform ideas had been developed under Chandra Shekhar with Yashwant Sinha as finance minister, but that government was short-lived. India was friendless after the USSR's fall, and Manmohan Singh quietly trekked between the India ED's office, the US Treasury and the IMF to get programmes moving. Percy Mistry worked his networks to speed up the money. A young Urjit Patel was negotiating on the IMF's side of the table, and Ashok Desai was chief economic adviser. Then came the July 1991 budget speech.
stories.insight: The reform that launched India 'into a different orbit' rested on unglamorous groundwork, built-up documentation and a quiet man doing the legwork when India counted for little.
stories.quote: And you have to remember at that time India was a dinky country. Like actually nobody gave a damn about India.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh in the Back Row, and at the Book Launch
stories.summary: Between his stints in power, Manmohan Singh was a private citizen in Delhi. Ajay, then a young researcher from Bombay giving talks, kept noticing him slip into the back seats, listen, and almost never speak or throw his weight around. In 2019, Vijay Kelkar invited him to release the first edition of Kelkar and Ajay's book In Service of the Republic. Manmohan Singh declined to be announced as chief guest because he was unwell and didn't want to derail the launch if he couldn't come. Then, without any announcement, he showed up, sat in the front row, shook Ajay's hand and told him it was a very important book.
stories.insight: Ajay sees this quiet decency as Manmohan Singh's method. He spent decades learning India's institutions, built coalitions gently, and moved a climate of opinion. Ajay calls that how a paradigm shifts, and he compares Manmohan Singh to Vajpayee in this respect.
stories.quote: He just took the trouble of coming and participating in these things.

stories.topic: Manmohan Singh Puts His Foot Down on the Nuclear Deal
stories.summary: In UPA-1, the Left parties supporting the government from outside threatened to pull out over the nuclear deal with the US. That was an existential risk to the government. Manmohan Singh refused to back down and got the deal through.
stories.insight: Amit uses it to show that accidental politicians can show real rectitude and courage once they are in the game.
stories.quote: He said, This is one thing I'm putting my foot down on.

stories.topic: Putin's Misreadings Before the Ukraine Invasion
stories.summary: Ajay argues Putin, a strongman 'deeply grounded in maleness', underestimated three things. He saw Zelenskyy as just a TV comedian. He looked at Western Europe's female defence ministers and thought 'they're women, what will they do?' And he read America's chaotic Afghanistan withdrawal as weakness: the US kept to a deal with the Taliban rather than staying longer for a managed exit. (Amit points out the withdrawal was botched under Biden; Ajay notes the dates were set by Trump.)
stories.insight: Strongman thinking mistakes the restraint and rule-following of liberal democracies, and talent in unfamiliar packaging, for weakness. Ajay sees these misjudgements as steps toward the mistake of February 2022.
stories.quote: Putin thought this guy's just a TV comedian. What will he do?

stories.topic: Zelenskyy: 'I Need Ammunition, Not a Ride'
stories.summary: Zelenskyy, a successful comedian, had played a president in a TV series. He then won 73% of the vote with an internet-heavy campaign as a clean outsider. When Russia invaded, Ajay expected the armoured thrust from Belarus to take Kyiv and Zelenskyy to flee to Lviv or run a government in exile from Poland. It is believed three separate assassination teams came for his house on the first night, with his wife and two small children there. Offered a way out, he said his place was here and he needed ammunition, not a ride.
stories.insight: His choice to stay showed Western countries that Ukraine would fight, and that is what made them willing to send military kit. Ajay says Zelenskyy made the right call every step of the way.
stories.quote: My place is here, I need ammunition, not a ride.

stories.topic: Roosevelt's Dying Envoy to Stalin
stories.summary: After Germany launched Operation Barbarossa in 1941, Roosevelt sent one of his most trusted advisers, who was dying of cancer, on a long route through Britain, North Africa and Iran to Moscow. His single task was to judge whether Stalin would stand and fight. The adviser met Stalin and sent back a short message: yes.
stories.insight: Before allies commit resources, they need to know the leader has the stomach for a fight. The West made the same judgement about Zelenskyy.
stories.quote: Otherwise, you know, you wouldn't support somebody who is emotionally and spiritually broken. You need to have stomach for the fight.

stories.topic: Demonetisation and the Paan Shop
stories.summary: Amit wrote a series of pieces against demonetisation, and one in the Times of India went viral: Rahul Gandhi and Kejriwal tweeted it, and an IT cell abused him for it. In it he took apart each of Modi's reasons. A key one was that Modi had been out of touch with daily life for decades. When Indira Gandhi demonetised in 1978, a thousand-rupee note was worth about twelve thousand rupees in 2016 terms. The 500-rupee note scrapped in 2016 was an everyday transaction note, and the cash-based informal economy was devastated.
stories.insight: Leaders cut off from ordinary transactions miss the texture of the economy. Amit argues an outsider with real-world experience would never have assumed poor people don't use 500-rupee notes.
stories.quote: This man has not bought something from a paan shop in fifteen years, and it matters because had he done so, he would have realized that a five hundred rupee note is not just a medium of storage.

stories.topic: George H.W. Bush Meets a Barcode Scanner
stories.summary: While running for election, Bush did a staged photo op at a supermarket checkout. When the cashier scanned an item and the price appeared instantly on the terminal, astonishment showed on his face, with the TV cameras rolling.
stories.insight: Elite life cuts leaders off from the ordinary world. Ajay's broader point is that real knowledge flows to leaders through conversations with people who aren't reverential toward them.
stories.quote: So this is a guy who for twenty five years had never stepped out to buy anything for himself.

recommendations.item: Havel: A Life
recommendations.creator: Michael Zantovsky
recommendations.context: Amit read from it while describing young Havel at the lab, in overalls with his pockets full of Kafka, Camus, Heidegger and Nietzsche.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great biography and finds a 'stirring' portrait of Havel's self-education in it.

recommendations.item: The Garden Party and Other Plays
recommendations.creator: Václav Havel
recommendations.context: Amit summarised The Garden Party, in which a young man rises to head a liquidation office by mastering content-free bureaucratic language until his own parents can't recognise him. He also discussed The Memorandum, built around an invented language designed for obfuscation.
recommendations.reason: He says they are hilarious, available in English and worth reading in full. The plays dramatise Havel's conviction that language shapes reality.

recommendations.item: Letters to Olga
recommendations.creator: Václav Havel
recommendations.context: Havel's letters to his wife during his years in prison.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it beautiful and quotes a line that sends a chill up his spine: 'If I am to be punished, let it be for who I am. If I am to be free, let it be as myself, not someone else's puppet.'

recommendations.item: The Power of the Powerless
recommendations.creator: Václav Havel
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode recommendation, alongside all of Havel's plays.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a wonderful extended essay and notes the latest edition has an introduction by Timothy Snyder, also worth reading.

recommendations.item: To the Castle and Back
recommendations.creator: Václav Havel
recommendations.context: Havel's memoir, recommended at the end.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a wonderful book.

recommendations.item: Charter 77
recommendations.creator: Václav Havel and co-signatories
recommendations.context: The 1977 dissident charter Havel co-authored, linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It is the document behind Havel's line to a hesitant signatory: 'you have already taken a side, just not the one that you think you have.'

recommendations.item: The Jackson Katz quote on passive sentence constructions
recommendations.creator: Jackson Katz
recommendations.context: Amit read it out to illustrate Havel's idea that language shapes reality.
recommendations.reason: It shows how the passive voice ('how many women were raped' rather than 'how many men raped women') takes the focus off the men committing violence.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Amit recalled Shrayana pointing out that men describe marriage as something they do, while women describe it as something that happens to them.
recommendations.reason: It is a close-to-home example of how everyday grammar robs women of agency.

recommendations.item: Salil Tripathi and the Gujaratis (Episode 409, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Salil Tripathi
recommendations.context: The episode where Salil told the story of asking Havel about free speech before his meeting with Lee Kuan Yew.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of one of the episode's best stories about Havel's moral clarity in power.

recommendations.item: Arvind Kejriwal's interview by Sudhir Chaudhary
recommendations.creator: Sudhir Chaudhary
recommendations.context: Amit contrasted Havel staying in his old flat with Kejriwal, who made noises about refusing an official bungalow and then had a palatial house refurbished.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an interesting interview in which Kejriwal is called out on his hypocrisy.

recommendations.item: Where Have All The Leaders Gone?
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Bloomberg Quint column on why India's freedom-fighter generation produced such outstanding leaders.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his incentive-based answer: those leaders entered politics as crusaders for principles, not as careerists chasing power and money.

recommendations.item: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947–1997
recommendations.creator: Salman Rushdie and Elizabeth West (eds.)
recommendations.context: Ajay noted that Rushdie's anthology opens with Tryst with Destiny.
recommendations.reason: Ajay says it makes sense that the speech is chapter one, because it is one of the transcendental pieces of Indian writing.

recommendations.item: Glimpses of World History
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Written as letters from jail to his daughter. It was one of the earliest books Ajay read, as a child.
recommendations.reason: It gave Ajay the feeling of a father telling stories to a daughter, exactly how his own father talked to him. He calls it a phenomenal book.

recommendations.item: The Discovery of India
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Discussed as part of Nehru's jail-time output.
recommendations.reason: Ajay considers it one of the most important theoretical books about India. It salvages an idea of India grounded in history and free of hatred, and sets up a modern synthesis comfortable with science and liberal democracy.

recommendations.item: A Tryst With Destiny
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Scribbled on tissue paper about fifteen minutes before it was delivered.
recommendations.reason: Ajay urges listeners to step out of the cliché and read it with fresh eyes, as transcendental writing.

recommendations.item: The Light Has Gone Out of Our Lives
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Ajay asked for Nehru's recording to be linked alongside Tryst with Destiny.
recommendations.reason: He says that raspy voice still does something to you across all these years.

recommendations.item: Letters to Chief Ministers
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Amit had been reading these before recording. He added them to Ajay's list of Nehru's books and later recommended all of Nehru's books.
recommendations.reason: They show a prime minister who wrote copiously and clearly. For Amit, that habit made Nehru a better thinker, and no modern politician of any party does it.

recommendations.item: The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi
recommendations.creator: Mahatma Gandhi
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned that Gandhi's 99 volumes are online.
recommendations.reason: He uses them to argue that India's founding leaders were great thinkers partly because they were prolific writers.

recommendations.item: The Collected Writings and Speeches of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar
recommendations.creator: B.R. Ambedkar
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside Gandhi's volumes. Ambedkar's 60-plus volumes are online.
recommendations.reason: Same argument: prolific writing went hand in hand with great thinking.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's 'mid-episode recommendation' after Ajay's account of Manmohan Singh.
recommendations.reason: It goes deep into the reforms Manmohan Singh steered.

recommendations.item: The 1991 Project
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Recommended alongside the 1991 reforms episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it absolutely fantastic, a treasure trove of material on 1991.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the people who were on the 1991 journey with Manmohan Singh.
recommendations.reason: It covers the other reformers of that era, though not Manmohan Singh himself.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Montek Singh Ahluwalia (Episode 285, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Montek Singh Ahluwalia
recommendations.context: Amit mentioned that Montek and other protagonists of 1991 had already been on his show. Manmohan Singh's health ruled out his own appearance.
recommendations.reason: A first-hand account from one of the key figures of 1991.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Manmohan Singh came unannounced to its 2019 launch and told Ajay it was a very important book. A second-edition paperback is now out.
recommendations.reason: It is the book Manmohan Singh personally endorsed, written by two people who worked inside India's policy process.

recommendations.item: Servant of the People
recommendations.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
recommendations.context: The TV series in which Zelenskyy, then a comedian, played a president before becoming one.
recommendations.reason: It is the improbable starting point of the most unlikely accidental-politician story.

recommendations.item: Volodymyr Zelenskyy playing the piano with his d***
recommendations.creator: Volodymyr Zelenskyy
recommendations.context: A clip from Zelenskyy's comedy days that Amit promised to show.
recommendations.reason: 'Excellent stuff, I love it.' It makes Amit's point that going on stage night after night to make a fool of yourself also takes courage.

recommendations.item: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
recommendations.context: The episode where Amit put to MR Madhavan the idea that politicians play three different games.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of his framework of electoral politics, intra-party/legislative politics, and governance.

recommendations.item: Narendra Modi takes a Great Leap Backwards
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's viral demonetisation piece, which took apart each of Modi's stated reasons.
recommendations.reason: It is his case study for why leaders without skin in the game of the real world make huge policy mistakes.

recommendations.item: The Insider
recommendations.creator: PV Narasimha Rao
recommendations.context: Amit noted that Narasimha Rao was an insider for decades, 'that's the name of his book.'
recommendations.reason: Rao's insider's political skill made Manmohan Singh's economics politically possible.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Greatness of PV Narasimha Rao (Episode 283, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Amit called it a great episode while discussing the Manmohan–Narasimha Rao partnership.
recommendations.reason: It explains why Rao deserves much of the credit for the 1991 reforms.

recommendations.item: Don't Run a Country Like a Company (Episode 60, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while discussing how outsiders struggle to find the levers of power.
recommendations.reason: It argues that policy-making is a completely different knowledge set from running a firm, and a hard one to acquire.

recommendations.item: Yes Minister
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
recommendations.context: Ajay's end-of-episode recommendation, prompted by the discussion of how complex governing is.
recommendations.reason: Among the loveliest and funniest books he has read, with genuine insight into real-world politics and the difficulty of change.

recommendations.item: Yes Prime Minister
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Lynn and Antony Jay
recommendations.context: Recommended together with Yes Minister.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls both of them masterpieces.

core_ideas.concept: Mature Institutions Make Expertise Portable, and Importable
core_ideas.explanation: A Canadian could run the Bank of England because advanced economies have sound measurement, good models, strong research teams and invisible checks and balances. Knowledge then travels across borders, in a kind of post-nationalism. India is different: the measurement is bad, the models barely exist and the RBI sits in a political mess, so expertise has to be rebuilt locally. Ajay applies the same logic to countries. East Germany 'cheated' by simply grabbing West German institutions. Poland imported some twenty thousand pages of EU rules on how to be a European country. Ukraine got no such machinery and inherited only the arbitrary violence of the USSR.
core_ideas.quote: So actually then the knowledge becomes portable.

core_ideas.concept: Political Parties Need to Be Depersonalised
core_ideas.explanation: India has paid too little attention to the political party as an institution. Like firms, parties need internal rules, norms, culture and a deep talent pool that outlasts individuals. The US has access points into politics at every level, from city to state to federal. Amit adds that Nehru's Congress worked this way, with chief ministers elected by legislators and able to refuse the PM, until Indira Gandhi hollowed it out.
core_ideas.quote: So just like we think of firms getting depersonalized, you need to think of political parties getting depersonalized.

core_ideas.explanation: Havel's plays show people losing their individuality by adopting empty bureaucratic language, and he told his actors that language shapes reality. Vague language hides what is happening and makes everything seem banal. Jackson Katz shows how the passive voice in 'violence against women' leaves out who is doing it. Shrayana Bhattacharya noted that women speak of marriage as something that happens to them, which robs them of agency.
core_ideas.quote: His whole point was that the language you use matters. That it has political importance, that it has moral importance.

core_ideas.explanation: Havel's lesson from Charter 77 and the Liu Xiaobo campaign echoes the line attributed to Edmund Burke. A citizen's duty is not only to refuse to cooperate with evil but also to speak up, because neutrality favours the powerful.
core_ideas.quote: So this tells you not only that your duty as a citizen is to not cooperate with the government, to not do evil. It also tells you that your duty is actually to speak up. That staying silent is also taking a side.

core_ideas.explanation: After the violence and lies of communism, or after Watergate, societies briefly crave a safe, ethical leader. That is when a poet like Havel, a Lech Walesa or a Jimmy Carter becomes possible. Soft moral power was also the only option against the USSR, just as fighting the British Empire needed a Gandhi rather than guns. Once the window closes, normal machine politics of polling booths and party organisation returns.
core_ideas.quote: After you've been through an orgy of bad behavior, every person just wants somebody who is safe.

core_ideas.concept: A Country Cannot Be Better Than Its Thinkers
core_ideas.explanation: A nation's thinkers set its production possibility frontier. A country can fall far below that frontier but cannot go beyond it. Post-communist Eastern Europe had its Havels and Walesas, and post-1947 India had Nehru, Gandhi and Ambedkar. Building a country from scratch, including choices like letting Slovakia go peacefully, depends on that intellectual and moral capability. Tyrants know this, which is why the Soviets killed Poland's thinkers at Katyn.
core_ideas.quote: A country can be much worse than its thinkers, but a country can't be better than its thinkers.

core_ideas.concept: Incentives and High Activation Energy Selected the Freedom Generation
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's answer to why India's first generation of leaders was so outstanding is incentives. They were crusaders for principles, not careerists, whereas today politics is rival mafias fighting for a monopoly on violence and it attracts that kind of person. Ajay adds a selection effect: taking on the British Empire was so costly that only the best jumped in, and then they found and argued with each other, as Gandhi did with Tagore.
core_ideas.quote: When you have to jump, a very high activation energy, only the best people will jump.

core_ideas.explanation: Postcolonial countries whose liberation movements took up guns tend to fall into repeated cycles of violence. India was lucky that its freedom movement sidelined the violent figures, Savarkar and Bose among them, and that Gandhi would call off a nationwide movement over violence at one police station. After 1947, Nehru's era firmly separated civilian rule from the military, so the army was never invited into power.

core_ideas.concept: The Strongman Pose Masks Inner Weakness
core_ideas.explanation: Nehru, even after nine years in jail, stayed a happy man who smiled, told jokes and made fun of himself. Ajay sees that comfort with oneself as a mark of great leaders. A secure person has nothing to prove, while the swagger of modern strongmen signals insecurity.
core_ideas.quote: This whole strongman mode that people put on, I think, is just a mask for your own inner weakness.

core_ideas.concept: Writing Is a Way of Thinking
core_ideas.explanation: Nehru wrote long letters to chief ministers, and Gandhi and Ambedkar left dozens of volumes. They were great thinkers partly because they were prolific writers. Writing, even in private, is how you engage with the world, understand yourself and shape your character. Amit laments that no modern Indian politician does this.
core_ideas.quote: These men were great thinkers in part because they were prolific writers and that is so important and something to admire.

core_ideas.concept: Hybrid Warfare: Turning a Country Against Itself
core_ideas.explanation: After 94% of Ukrainians voted for independence in 1991, Russia kept interfering. It backed and armed a pro-Russian party and fomented polarisation, conflict and anger so the country stayed weak.
core_ideas.quote: The game of modern hybrid warfare is to pit a country against itself.

core_ideas.explanation: From Amit's conversation with MR Madhavan: a politician in government plays three separate games. The first is electoral politics, reading the public pulse and winning votes, a skill Amit says we shouldn't disdain. The second is politics within the party and the legislature. The third is governance, running ministries, bureaucracies and institutions. Skill in one predicts little about the others, and Churchill, a war winner booted out in peace, is the reminder. So Amit's answer on whether Zelenskyy can win a post-war election is that we simply don't know.
core_ideas.quote: A politician who comes to government is not playing one game, they are playing three different games.

core_ideas.explanation: A career politician, especially in India, may never have had a paying job and doesn't know the outside world. Bankers, lawyers and businesspeople bring domain knowledge and respect for enterprise. Someone who chooses to leave a successful career for politics also tends to have wider interests than their peers.
core_ideas.quote: We could easily channel the spirits of Kipling and C. L. R. James and say what do they know of politics who only politics know.

core_ideas.concept: Skin in the Game, and Unreverential Friends
core_ideas.explanation: Outsiders have lived in the real world and may have been on the receiving end of bad policy, while insulated careerists produce errors like demonetisation. Ajay adds that knowledge reaches leaders mainly through conversations. A Havel or a Zelenskyy arrives with a large network of real people who aren't reverential toward a new head of state and will tell it straight.
core_ideas.quote: And those real human beings are not reverential because you've just become a head of state.

core_ideas.concept: Independent Directors as Funnels of Information
core_ideas.explanation: Companies need a majority of independent directors because inside the firm the CEO's power breeds groupthink and kills dissent. Each independent director brings in the blunt opinions of dozens of outsiders. Ajay argues every government organisation should have a majority of independent directors who are genuinely private people, not retired civil servants, because the state tends to have a very narrow view of the world.
core_ideas.quote: Because each of them is a funnel. And they're bringing voices inside, and that's where the information lies.

core_ideas.explanation: An outsider with a career to fall back on can be more equanimous and less brutal, since losing power won't destroy them. Ajay extends this to whole systems: if losing an election means jail, people fight elections far more dirtily. Vijay Kelkar's ideal is power dispersed so that it is never winner-takes-all.
core_ideas.quote: So a good society is one where elections are low stakes. So Kelkar always says that in a good society, politicians should go out of office, but never out of power.

core_ideas.explanation: Contesting elections in India costs crores even at corporator level. Funders expect a return on investment through contracts, protection from competition such as FDI in retail, and roads that grow potholes again so the repair contract comes back. Career politicians are locked into this repeated game. Outsiders haven't played it as long, so they have slightly more room to stay clean, and Ajay adds that a lifetime of forged character makes it hard to become a mere deal-maker.
core_ideas.quote: To survive in politics you need money, money will demand ROI. It is straight away corruption.

core_ideas.concept: Technocrat Plus Politician: The Manmohan–Narasimha Rao Partnership
core_ideas.explanation: Outsiders struggle to navigate politics and bureaucracy. In 1991 Manmohan Singh knew exactly what to do economically and had a team in place, while Narasimha Rao, an insider for decades, handled the manoeuvres, compromises and negotiations. Amit thinks Manmohan was right as finance minister but might have been wrong as prime minister at that moment. Ajay recalls the UK Labour insider who said that on coming to power after a long spell out, 'we pressed the levers of power and nothing happened.'
core_ideas.quote: Narasimha Rao could do the politics and Manmohan could do the economics.

core_ideas.concept: Outsiders and Parties Want Different Levels of Risk
core_ideas.explanation: Career politicians face elections again and again over decades, so they lean toward the status quo and avoid high-variance bets. An outsider whose legacy is already made may want a bold gamble for a grand success. These subtly misaligned incentives make it hard for an outsider to carry a party over the long run.
core_ideas.quote: If you are going to remain in the party for the next thirty years, you don't wanna play a high variance game, you don't wanna rock the boat.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit asks whether Ajay would accept absolute power, given that 'power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely.' Ajay: 'Power corrupts, but absolute power is pretty cool… get a better constitution of India. What better use of absolute power?'
Ajay borrows the lyric 'imagine there's no country, it's easy if you try' to describe the post-nationalist world that let a Canadian run the Bank of England.
Ajay on Watergate as the scandal that led to Jimmy Carter: 'Oh how helpless we were in those days, we thought that those are dreadful things. Standards of crime have changed.'
Ajay on rebuilding post-communist Europe: 'East Germany is cheating because it just grabbed West German institutions.'

Amit on Havel inviting Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones instead of summitry: 'I can have important conferences and World Economic Forum and this forum and that forum and that committee and G eighteen and B fifty nine, I'm just making shit up… but it's Frank Zappa and the Rolling Stones.'

Amit voices Havel's tie refusal in Hindi ('Tie nahi pehnunga… chalis saal se… kyun change karu?'), then adds: 'of course not in Hindi, because while he was a very learned man, he was not aware of this particular language.'
Jimmy Carter was the first American president to wear jeans in public. Amit pairs this with Havel's disdain for presidential dress codes.
Amit on what a 20-year-old Nehru would do today: not politics, 'maybe he would be an intern at XKDR Forum. Who knows?'
Amit on Gandhi choosing Nehru over the free-market-loving Rajaji because Nehru was much younger: 'So it's ironic that Rajaji actually outlived Nehru.'
Ajay on Nehru's nine years in British jails, kept in decent conditions. Amit: 'It was pretty luxurious jail.'

Amit praising Manmohan Singh's nuclear deal: 'I also admire the economist who will go unnamed, who sent a memo to the Prime Minister's office outlining why such a nuclear deal should happen, after which it happened.' This is a dig at Ajay, whose memos Amit had earlier said he 'can't speak about in public.'

After the shoot moved indoors: 'We have shifted indoors because a war started outside. No, a war did not start outside… the sun went down. So the sun hasn't gone down on Ukraine yet,' as the segue to Zelenskyy.

Ajay: 'O ye Namsita and Vaishnav, O ye little bit players of Bollywood, can you imagine that a comedian in Indian tinsel town can stand up and achieve such character.' Amit: 'They are future superstars of world cinema. So kindly hold your horses. Do you have any horses? Acquire horses and hold them there.'

Amit on Zelenskyy's unmatched credential: 'Churchill cannot compare. Nehruji cannot compare. Havel for all his skills in theatre cannot compare. Zelenskyy played the piano with his dick.' He adds that making a fool of yourself on stage night after night also takes courage.
Ajay on Zelenskyy rallying his people, citing the line about Churchill that 'he picked up the words of the English language and hurled them into battle.'
Amit on outsiders: 'You could be a chaiwala, as long as you're an actual chaiwala selling chai at a train station.'
Amit on election costs: 'I was gonna say shit ton of money. It's fine, I can say it, it's my show.'

Amit's limerick on politics, from his days as the Times of India's weekly limerick writer ('the world's only paid limerick writer, I think'): 'A neta who loves currency notes / told me what his line of work denotes. / It is kind of funny, we steal people's money / and use some of it to buy their votes.'
Amit quotes the line attributed to Edmund Burke, 'The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to stand by and do nothing,' as a mirror of Havel's Charter 77 retort.
Amit adapts Kipling and C.L.R. James: 'What do they know of politics who only politics know?'

Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican candidate, is Amit's example of the US norm of business people entering politics: 'those were the days you had good candidates from both parties. Look at today, it's just a joke.'

Ajay on the freedom fighters taking on the British Empire: 'you and whose army?' They had to be crazy people. And when such people argue, as Gandhi did with Tagore, 'you're going to build something great out of it.'
Ajay recalls a Labour insider after the party returned to power in the UK: 'we pressed the levers of power and nothing happened.'

Amit's sign-off after asking viewers to like and subscribe: 'You know they don't listen to me. This is why I could never win as a politician. No one would vote for me. They might like me, but they won't vote for me.' Ajay repeats the request; Amit: 'Let's hope you're better at this than I am.'
